title: Thermalization-Controlled Superconducting Diode-Like Transport in Disordered Molybdenum and NbN Thin Films
authors: Akhilesh Kumar, Shivani Soni, Gomathi Natarajan, Ramanathaswamy Pandian, Thameemul Ansari M, Pooja Gupta, Sanjay Rai, Edward Prabu Amaladass
abstract: Superconducting diode effects are characterized by direction-dependent critical currents in the superconducting state. Here, we investigate diode-like transport in 128-nm-thick Mo thin film deposited on Si_SiO2 substrate by DC magnetron sputtering. The thin film exhibit a superconducting transition temperature TC of 5.8 K. Pronounced current-direction asymmetry and hysteresis are observed in current-voltage characteristics measured in a closed-cycle refrigerator. In contrast, the same thin film exhibits a substantially more symmetric response in a 14T cryogenic system with improved sample thermalization. We attribute this strong dependence on the measurement environment to electrothermal effects arising from current-induced Joule heating and finite thermal relaxation. As the current approaches the superconducting-to-resistive switching condition, the emergence of a resistive component leads to a rapid increase in Joule heating, raising the sample temperature and modifying the switching condition. Conversely, during the resistive-to-superconducting transition, residual heating and finite thermal relaxation reduce the switching current. Since P is equal to I2R it is independent of current polarity, the observed asymmetry is not associated with polarity-dependent Joule heating but with the interplay of thermal relaxation, sweep history, and thermal boundary conditions. The suppression of the asymmetry under improved thermalization, together with similar behavior observed in NbN reference films, indicates that the apparent diode-like response is strongly influenced by electrothermal effects. These results highlight the need to distinguish thermal switching and hysteresis from intrinsic nonreciprocal superconductivity when identifying superconducting diode effects in transport measurements.
summary: This work examines superconducting diode effects in Mo thin films, initially observing strong current-direction asymmetry. By comparing results from different thermal environments and using thermal simulations, the authors conclude that the apparent diode behavior is largely an artifact of electrothermal feedback from Joule heating. This highlights the critical need to decouple thermal switching from true intrinsic non-reciprocal superconductivity.
main_problem: The paper investigates the origin of superconducting diode effects (direction-dependent critical currents) in thin films, aiming to distinguish intrinsic non-reciprocal superconductivity from measurement artifacts.
main_result: The observed current-direction asymmetry is primarily attributed to electrothermal effects arising from Joule heating and finite thermal relaxation, rather than an intrinsic superconducting non-reciprocity.
method: The study combines electrical transport measurements (I-V curves) in different cryogenic environments with thermal modeling (Energy 2D simulations) to analyze heat dissipation pathways.
model_or_system: The physical systems studied are superconducting thin films, specifically Mo and NbN, deposited on Si/SiO2 substrates, which exhibit superconducting transitions around 5.8 K.
key_observables: Current-direction asymmetry ($\Delta I_c$), critical current density ($J_c$), and the dependence of transport characteristics on the measurement environment (e.g., thermalization level).
important_parameters: Superconducting transition temperature ($T_C \approx 5.8$ K), current density ($I$), and the thermal relaxation time/boundary conditions.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption tested is that the observed asymmetry can be modeled by thermal feedback ($P=I^2R$) rather than solely by microscopic symmetry breaking mechanisms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the temperature dependence of resistance and I-V curves showing asymmetry in a closed-cycle refrigerator (CCR) versus a 14T system. Simulations compare heat transfer under different cooling conditions, showing the impact of convection.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by presenting initial observations of asymmetry in Mo films, contrasting these results between two different cryogenic setups, attributing the discrepancy to electrothermal effects, and concluding with simulations that model the thermal feedback mechanism.
why_interesting: The rigorous separation of intrinsic quantum effects from classical thermal/dissipative effects is crucial for interpreting measurements in superconducting quantum devices, linking macroscopic transport to microscopic physics.
